bio.en: Melanie Perkins is the co-founder and CEO of Canva, the design platform valued at over $42 billion, on track to be one of the most successful founders in tech history.
bio.zh: 梅兰妮·珀金斯（Melanie Perkins）是 Canva 的联合创始人兼 CEO，这家设计平台估值超过 420 亿美元，有望成为科技史上最成功的创始人之一。

summary.en: Melanie recounts pitching over 100 investors who all said no, and turning each rejection into a new slide that sharpened her market thesis. She champions "crazy big goals" that make you feel inadequate and thus work harder to will them into existence. The episode is an inspiring founder story about persistence, vision, and betting on yourself.
summary.zh: 梅兰妮讲述了她向 100 多位投资人 pitch 却全部被拒，并把每一次拒绝变成一张新幻灯片、从而打磨出更清晰市场论点的经历。她推崇能让你自觉不足、从而更拼命去实现的"疯狂大目标"。本期是一则关于坚持、远见与押注自己的励志创始人故事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's a very famous story about Canva. Early on, you pitched over a hundred investors and over a hundred investors said no to you.
turns.zh: 关于Canva有一个非常著名的故事。早期的时候，你向一百多个投资者推销产品，结果一百多个投资者都拒绝了你。

turns.speaker: Melanie Perkins
turns.en: It was really clear in my mind that it was the future and I thought the investors were wrong, frankly. But investors also gave really helpful feedback and feedback. Often in the form of rejection, they would say, "Oh, your market's not big enough," and I would say, "It's going to be huge." And I'd add a new page in my pitch deck that said how big the market I believe was, and then they'd say, "You're the same as some of other company." And I would say, "Hey, now I've got a new slide in my pitch deck that shows all the players and the huge gap in the market that we believe we're going to fill."
turns.zh: 在我看来，那就是未来的趋势。说实话，我当时觉得那些投资者错了。不过投资者也给了我很有用的反馈，通常以拒绝的形式。他们会说：“哦，你的市场规模不够大。”我会说：“它会变得非常庞大。”然后我在推介文档里加一页，说明我认为市场规模有多大，接着他们会说：“你和其他公司没什么两样。”我会说：“嘿，我在推介文档里新加了一页，展示了所有市场参与者，以及我们认为自己将填补的巨大市场空白。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: One of your values, Crazy Big Goals. I love that as a value.
turns.zh: 你们的价值观之一是“疯狂的宏伟目标”。我很喜欢这个价值观。

turns.speaker: Melanie Perkins
turns.en: The thing that I love about a crazy big goal is that you feel completely inadequate before it. You want to work really hard to will it into existence. I really like to start by just imagining what is the future that you actually want Right now? I have a wall in my house in my office, which is my vision for what I'd like the world to look like in 2050.
turns.zh: 我喜欢疯狂宏伟目标的地方在于，在它面前你会感到自己完全不够格。你会为了让它成真而拼命努力。我喜欢先想象一下你真正想要的未来是什么样子。我的办公室里有一面墙，上面写着我对2050年世界面貌的构想。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I heard from one of your team members, Melissa Tan, there's a deck like this for every project you kick off. There's this big vision deck.
turns.zh: 我从你们团队成员梅丽莎·陈那里听说，每个你们启动的项目都有这样一个推介文档。就是这样一个宏伟愿景文档。

turns.speaker: Melanie Perkins
turns.en: So we have this concept of chaos to clarity. Every idea starts in the chaos side, and then you have to work all the way to the other side, which is clarity. That very first step at the far end of chaos was quite an embarrassing step actually, because you don't have mastery at that point. You don't have all the answers.
turns.zh: 所以我们有从混乱到清晰的概念。每个想法都从混乱的阶段开始，然后你要一步步走向清晰的阶段。在混乱的极端阶段迈出的第一步其实挺尴尬的，因为那时你还没有掌握足够的知识，也没有所有的答案。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: A lot of people think of Canva as like design graphics for social media and marketing and things like that, but you also have spreadsheets, whiteboards, charts, AI coding tool.
turns.zh: 很多人认为Canva就是做社交媒体和营销用的设计图之类的，但你们还有电子表格、白板、图表、AI编码工具。

turns.speaker: Melanie Perkins
turns.en: Was funny, looking back from really old decks. We were trying to do AI before AI was actually a thing.
turns.zh: 回看以前的旧文档挺有意思的。我们当时就试图做AI，而那时候AI还根本不算是个热门领域。

turns.speaker: Melanie Perkins
turns.en: Thank you so much for having me. I'm excited to be here.
turns.zh: 非常感谢您邀请我。能来到这里我感到很兴奋。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm even more excited. It's such an honor to have you here. I am such a fan of yours. I'm such a fan of the company that you've built. Also just everyone I meet from Canva is just so nice and so awesome and so smart, and so clearly you've built something really special. I'm really excited to use this hour to learn as much as I can from you about how you did that. We were actually chatting ahead of this about what would make the best use of this hour. I asked you what you believe has been the biggest factor in the success of Canva. You described something called building a Column B company and Column B thinking, I've never heard of this before, so let us start there. What is building Column B company, what does that mean?
turns.zh: 我甚至更加激动。您能来到这里真是荣幸之至。我是您的忠实粉丝，也是您所创立的这家公司的忠实拥趸。还有，我在Canva遇到的每一个人都非常友善、才华横溢、智慧过人，而且显然您打造了非凡的事业。我非常期待利用这一个小时尽可能多地向您学习如何做到这一点。实际上，我们在会前讨论了如何充分利用这一个小时。我问您，您认为Canva成功的最关键因素是什么？您提到了"打造 Column B 型公司"和 Column B 思维模式，我之前从未听说过，所以让我们从这里开始。什么是 Column B 型公司？这意味着什么？

turns.speaker: Melanie Perkins
turns.en: Really great place to start. So I guess there's two ways of planning. The way that you can plan is you can dream of what is the perfect vision of the future, what future do you want to exist in, what would you like the world to look like? What would you like companies to look like? And then going from there, which is completely improbable, a completely crazy big dream, and then working hard to turn that into reality. And the alternate is, so just imagine you are building a castle on the hill and you're like, "What would be the most magical, wonderful, mythical experience?" And the other thing you can do is you can look at the bricks around you and you can say, "What can I do with these bricks? How high can I stack them? What can I do?" And I think most planning is often done by looking at the bricks and trying to stack them, and then you can create only so much. And so I guess the column B thinking is thinking about what is that magical wonderful future that you then want to invest years and decades of your life actually building? And so that's column A and column B in a nutshell.
turns.zh: 这确实是个很好的切入点。规划的方式有两种：一种是设想未来最理想的愿景，描绘出您希望生活在怎样的未来，希望世界变成什么样，公司又该如何运作？然后从这个完全不切实际、近乎疯狂的宏伟梦想出发，努力将其变为现实。另一种方式是想象自己在山上建造一座城堡，问自己："最神奇、最美妙、最具传奇色彩的体验会是怎样的？"然后利用身边现有的砖块，思考如何堆叠它们？我认为大多数规划往往是从现有资源出发，试图垒高砖块，但创造的空间毕竟有限。所以 Column B 思维模式就是思考您理想中的未来愿景，愿意为之投入数年乃至数十年时间去打造。这就是 Column A 和 Column B 的核心区别。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So column A is the traditional just work from today's world. Column B is work from this dream reality and work backwards from how to achieve that.
turns.zh: 所以 Column A 是当下职场的常规模式，Column B 则是在梦想现实中逆向设计实现目标的路径。

turns.speaker: Melanie Perkins
turns.en: Exactly that.
turns.zh: 没错，就是这样。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is exactly the way actually Brian Chesky thought. I worked at Airbnb for a long time and it was always just, "Think about the world, the dream and then work backwards from that," so there's a lot clearly also worked out. So clearly this is an important lesson in the example of Canva, just what would've been column A for what Canva could have been and how did you think about the column B approach of what Canva in a dreamland could be?
turns.zh: 这正是布莱恩·切斯基（Brian Chesky）的思维方式。我在Airbnb工作多年，公司一直秉持"先构想理想世界，再逆向设计实现路径"的理念，显然这种方法行之有效。Canva的案例中，这一点体现得尤为明显——如果Canva停留在 Column A 阶段，可能会错失哪些机遇？又是如何通过 Column B 思维模式构想理想中的Canva呢？

turns.speaker: Melanie Perkins
turns.en: So column A would've been nothing frankly, because the reality was when I was a university student with no company and no business or product or software experience, the reality would've been not very much. And so it was all column B, it was all thinking about the wild future that we wanted to create. Imagine what would be publishing in the future, what would communications look like in the future? And it seemed really impossible that it would stay on the desktop, it would stay really complicated. And it just seemed so apparent to me that in the future it was going to be completely different. Could I build that future? I had absolutely no idea, but the idea, it seemed completely likely, completely improbable that it wouldn't be the case that in the future, design would be online and collaborative and really simple. And so starting from that, we then took that concept and applied it to the school yearbook market in Australia with our first company Fusion Books. And then we applied it to Canva where we wanted to take it much, much bigger.
turns.zh: 坦白说，A列本质上毫无意义，因为现实情况是，当我还是一名大学生，没有公司、没有商业经验、没有产品或软件开发经验时，A列确实一无是处。于是全部希望都寄托在B列上——我们畅想未来将创造怎样的奇迹。想象未来出版业会是什么样子，通信领域又会迎来怎样的革新？当时人们普遍认为传统桌面应用仍将占据主导地位，操作极其复杂。然而我深信未来必将焕然一新。能否亲手缔造这个未来？我当时毫无头绪，但这个构想却充满可能性——如果未来设计能实现在线化、协作化且操作简便，那又何尝不可？正是基于此，我们创立了首家公司Fusion Books，将这一理念引入澳大利亚校园年册市场，随后又将其应用于Canva平台，力图将其规模进一步扩大。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let's talk about just how to actually go about building a Column B company. Say a founder is listening to this and they're just like, "Okay, I want to do this." What do they do? What are the steps? Where do you start?
turns.zh: 接下来让我们探讨如何真正打造B列公司。假设有创业者听完后心想：“好吧，我要行动了。”该如何着手？步骤是什么？从何入手？

turns.speaker: Melanie Perkins
turns.en: I really like to start by just imagining what is the future that you actually want? What is the world that you want to live in? What is the future of transportation? What is the future of healthcare? What is the future that you want to live in and exist in? And for example, right now I have a wall in my house in my office, which is my vision for what I'd like the world to look like in 2050. And so it's not necessarily that you can bring that into existence or you can will that into existence, but just to start to get clearer on what you would like that world to be like. Would you like it to be more inclusive? Would you like it? For me, one of the things I desperately want is everyone on this planet to have their basic human needs met. (00:08:56): What are those things that you believe are so important that you would love to see exist in that future? And I think an exercise we often do is what is wild success for X, or what is wild success for Y? And then equally, what is terrible failure for those things? And you can apply that just to abstract thinking in different industries. You can do that, apply that. We do that for the whole company for different areas of the company. And I think just taking that very long timescale of 10 years and getting a really crisp idea of what you want, of what you don't want, that's sort of the first step. And I think a lot of people don't spend quite enough time imagining that. And then the next part is you don't want to just have this crazy big dream and then do nothing about turning it into reality. (00:09:43): You kind of want to have a ladder that goes all the way up to the moon, which is your crazy, wild vision. And then you want to have rungs that just work its way up step by step. And so you want to get that really clear picture of the future that you would like and then just take little step, after little step, after little step. And it doesn't matter how small that first step is or how seemingly inconsequential if it is working towards that future that you want to will into existence, then you'll keep on climbing up that ladder in the right direction.
turns.zh: 我通常会从畅想理想未来开始：你希望生活在怎样的世界？交通的未来会是怎样的？医疗领域又将迎来哪些变革？你渴望身处怎样的未来？比如，我办公室墙上挂着我对2050年世界愿景的构想。当然，现实中未必能完全实现这些构想，但至少要先清晰自己的理想图景。理想中的世界应更包容、更公正。对我而言，最迫切的愿望是让地球上每个人都能满足基本生存需求。（00:08:56）：你认为哪些未来愿景至关重要？我们常问：X的成功上限在哪里，Y的失败极限又在哪里？这种思维方式适用于不同行业的抽象思考。我们在公司内部各部门也采用这种方法。关键在于以十年为长远视角，清晰界定理想与非理想目标——这才是第一步。遗憾的是，许多人缺乏这种想象力。接下来要避免空想大而不切实际的愿景，却无所作为。（00:09:43）：你需要像攀登月球般的宏伟愿景，也要脚踏实地的一步步攀升。先描绘出理想图景，再分解成可行的步骤。即使第一步微不足道，只要朝着愿景前进，终将登上正确的阶梯。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think a lot of people hearing this might feel like, "I do this. Yeah, I have a vision. I know where I'm going. I have this big idea." What do you think they might be missing about just what this actually means and why they're probably not thinking big enough, they're not making the time to think this.
turns.zh: 我觉得很多人听到这话可能会觉得，"我也这样啊。对，我有愿景。我知道自己要去哪儿。我有个宏伟的想法。"但你可能忽略了其中的关键——人们往往没意识到这意味着什么，也没意识到自己为什么没能真正放开格局、抽出时间去思考。

turns.speaker: Melanie Perkins
turns.en: I think it is easy to be discouraged by the two, because they're completely two complete odds. They're completely different ends of the spectrum. So one is dreaming about the future, not that you think you can will into existence, it's just the future that you want. And then the next part is taking the tiny step that might be extremely microscopic and it feels a little embarrassing to be like, "I want a future that is," whatever it might be. And then to take such a microscopic step because I think you often have the future in one side or don't spend much time thinking about that. You're just thinking about the bricks before you. And so I think it's also naturally we all get distracted by day-to-day. It's your email, your Slack, the things that are kind of in your face, the reality that lives around you every day that kind of pulls you into this moment right now. (00:11:14): And so I think actually just making time to spend thinking about that is probably one of the most critical pieces. Just literally dreaming what is wild success in 10 years, what is terrible failure in 10 years is a really great place to start, is just spending some time there. And then even if that is so big and so vast and so wild, having that very first step is so important because then you take that little tiny first step and then the next step then that compounds for us, it's been compounding over a decade as we continue to work towards that same mission and vision.
turns.zh: 我觉得人们很容易被这两种状态困扰，因为它们完全南辕北辙，截然相反。一端是畅想未来，尽管你不认为能凭意志召唤未来，但你至少对未来有所向往；另一端是踏出微小却至关重要的第一步。比如你想拥有某种未来，却觉得那微不足道，甚至有些难为情。人们往往要么沉浸在未来，要么无暇顾及，只专注于眼前的事务。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to hear how you operationalize this. I heard from one of your team members, Melissa Tan, that there's a deck like this for every project you kick off. There's this big vision deck. Talk about what that looks like, because I think that's where people are like, "Okay, how do I actually do this?" Talk about that deck.
turns.zh: 我想听听你们如何将这些理念付诸实践。我从团队成员梅丽莎·谭那里得知，你们每个新项目都会制作这样一份愿景文件。能否讲讲具体内容？因为人们往往会问："好吧，我该怎么做？"请分享一下这份文件的结构。

turns.speaker: Melanie Perkins
turns.en: So we have this concept of chaos to clarity and every idea starts in the chaos side, and then you have to work all the way to the other side, which is clarity. And so chaos can be an idea, it can be a problem, it can be a philosophy or a belief. And I've got a joke that I find funny. I'm not sure if you will, but how do you go from chaos to clarity? You add clarity. And so the idea is that each little step from chaos to clarity is the very first step might be literally writing it down. So rather than it being in your head, you've written it down, then the next step might be starting to create a pitch deck on it. And the next step might be starting to refine that, turning it into some designs, turning into a prototype. And then as it kind of goes from chaos to clarity, it starts to become more and more real and more and more people can see it. And so just taking those little incremental steps that adds clarity with every single step, then starts to help will it into existence rather than it being something that's completely amorphous and just stays in your head. So I think that's why visual communication for us is so important, is because otherwise, if it's just in your head, no one else can see it and you can't will it into existence.
turns.zh: 我们提倡从混乱到清晰的转变，每个创意都始于混乱阶段，之后逐步走向清晰。混乱可以是某个想法、某个问题、某种理念或信仰。我有个自以为有趣的玩笑：如何从混乱走向清晰？答案是增加清晰度！关键在于，从混乱到清晰的每一步都至关重要，比如最初的记录，再到制作推介文案，接着优化设计，直至打造原型。随着清晰度不断提升，创意逐渐具象化，越来越多人能理解它。正是这些循序渐进的清晰度积累，最终让创意从虚无缥缈变为现实。因此，视觉化沟通对我们至关重要，否则创意只停留在脑海中，既无法被他人理解，也难以落地生根。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This makes me think about this concept of an ugly baby from the book, Creativity Inc., by I think Ed Catmull where he talks about how new ideas or this ugly baby that nobody wants to look at and deal with that I think he says they want to kill. I don't know why you would do that with an ugly baby. But there are these very soft, fragile things and it's really important to not kill them early and give them a chance to survive. And it's kind what I'm hearing here is have this big vision that many people are be like, "No, wait. This is completely absurd." And I love this idea of, "Okay, but here's one step we could take there to see if this could be a thing."
turns.zh: 这让我想起了《创意公司》一书中提到的"丑陋婴儿"概念。埃德·卡特穆尔在书中谈到，新想法就像"没人愿意看、没人愿意处理的丑陋婴儿"，他甚至说人们会想"干脆杀了它"。但我实在不明白为什么要对丑陋的婴儿下手。不过，有些脆弱易碎的事物确实很重要，不能过早扼杀它们，而是要给它们生存的机会。听起来这里的核心观点是，拥有宏大愿景时，很多人会说："不，等等，这简直太荒谬了。"而我喜欢这样的理念："好吧，但我们可以先迈出一步，看看这能否成真。"

turns.speaker: Melanie Perkins
turns.en: Yeah, I completely agree. And I think that's the thing is that that very first step at the very far end of chaos, it's very embarrassing because you're like, "I have this idea that is so big and so wild and how the hell would I do that? I have no idea." And so it's quite a embarrassing step, actually, because you don't have mastery at that point. You don't have all the answers. In fact, you have likely none of the answers, but you just have the idea that you think would be cool. And ideally you get the idea that it would be so cool that you want to work really hard to will that into existence. And so I think one of the really key parts is not only just having the idea but thinking it's so cool that you're going to work for years to will it into existence. Actually Melissa did a really amazing pitch deck recently about the vision of, I won't go into the details right here, but the vision of her space and I was really excited about it. And so I think that that's the great thing about a pitch deck, is that other people can see your thinking and your thinking actually gets clarified as well as you go through that process.
turns.zh: 是的，我完全赞同。我觉得关键在于，在混乱的边缘迈出第一步时，那会让人很尴尬，因为你会想："我有这个既宏大又疯狂的想法，可我该怎么实现它呢？我毫无头绪。"实际上，那是相当令人尴尬的一步，因为那时你还没有掌握技巧，无法给出所有答案。事实上，你很可能一无所知，但你只是有了一个觉得很酷的想法。理想情况下，你会觉得这个想法非常棒，愿意为之付出巨大努力去实现它。所以我认为关键点不仅在于有想法，还在于你要坚信这个想法足够酷，愿意为之奋斗多年。实际上，梅丽莎最近做了一个非常棒的Pitch Deck，讲的是她的愿景，我在这里就不详细说明了，但我对她的构想非常兴奋。所以我觉得Pitch Deck的妙处就在于，通过这个过程，其他人能看到你的思考，而你自己的思考也会因此变得更加清晰。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I talked to Melissa, I talked to a bunch of other people that work at Canva, that have worked at Canva, and something else I heard along these lines is this phrase, Crazy Big Goals, which I think is one of your values. Crazy Big Goals. I love that as a value. Why is that so important? How does that fit into this? And just talk about the power of having Crazy Big Goals.
turns.zh: 我和梅丽莎以及其他许多在Canva工作过的人聊过天，我听到的另一个观点是"疯狂大目标"，我认为这是你们的价值观之一。疯狂大目标。我很欣赏这个价值观。为什么它如此重要？它如何与这里所说的相契合？就谈谈拥有疯狂大目标的力量吧。

turns.speaker: Melanie Perkins
turns.en: Yeah, so right from the start of Canva, it was truly a crazy-big goal. We're like, "We want to empower the world of design and take all these things that are super complicated and put them into one platform and make it accessible to the whole world. And we want to, rather than it be super expensive and unaffordable, we want to empower everyone everywhere in the world to design." So I mean, that was the epitome of a crazy big goal. And if we macro out even further, we've got this two-step plan, build one of the world's most valuable companies and do the most good we can do. So again, a rather crazy big goal. And I think the thing that I love about a crazy big goal is that you feel completely inadequate before it. Another crazy big goal. We'd love to see everyone's basic human needs met on the planet. Completely crazy big, that truly shouldn't be. It's kind of absolutely absurd that that's the case, but we can go into that later. (00:16:02): But I think with a crazy big goal, then you want to work really hard to will it into existence. And so if you start with a reasonable goal or a realistic goal, then you kind of get to it and you're like, "Oh cool, whatever." Or more importantly, if something happens, all the problems and roadblocks come along as they always do, then you're like, "Okay, I won't bother with that." And then you can just go and choose another course. And so a crazy big goal is both crazy big, but it's also something that you think is incredibly important that you actually want to will into existence because it is so much work to will a crazy big goal into existence. So it better be one that you want to actually achieve.
turns.zh: 是的，从Canva创立之初，这就是一个极其宏大的目标。我们当时就想：“我们要赋予全球设计力量，将那些极其复杂的工具整合到一个平台上，让全世界都能用上设计工具。我们要让设计不再高不可攀，而是让地球上的每一个人都能轻松设计。” 这就是一个典型的疯狂大目标。再往大了说，我們有两个阶段性的目标：打造全球最具价值的公司，并尽可能创造最大的社会价值。所以这又是一个相当疯狂的大目标。我觉得疯狂大目标的魅力在于，在目标实现之前，你会感到自己能力不足。还有一个疯狂大目标——我们希望地球上的每个人都能满足基本生存需求。这听起来简直不可思议，但现实却如此残酷。不过这个话题我们可以稍后再谈。（00:16:02）但我认为，对于疯狂大目标，你必须全力以赴将其变为现实。如果你一开始设定的是一个合理或现实的目标，那么当你真正着手时，你可能会觉得“哦，随便吧”。更重要的是，如果遇到问题或障碍，你很可能会想“算了，不理会了”，然后转而选择其他方向。因此，疯狂大目标不仅规模宏大，而且你必须深信其重要性，才能倾注全部精力去实现它，因为将疯狂大目标变为现实需要付出巨大的努力。所以它必须是真正值得你为之奋斗的目标。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there a crazy big goal that you set that comes to mind maybe as a good example of, "This is what I'm talking about?" Maybe a product you launched or feature back in the day?
turns.zh: 你有没有设定过什么疯狂大目标？能举个例子说明“这就是我所说的”吗？比如你推出的某个产品或功能？

turns.speaker: Melanie Perkins
turns.en: Yeah, I mean so many things. So we have our mission to empower the world to design and we break it down into mission pillars. So empower everyone to design anything with every ingredient in every language on every device, obviously a mouthful. But then what we do is we take successive goals every year towards this mission. And so for designing anything, we started off with social media and presentations and docs and websites and whiteboards and video. And so every year we're just launching more and more things to fulfill that part of the mission of empowering everyone to design anything. And then equally in every language we started in English and then it was Spanish and then it was 20 languages and then a hundred languages and then hard languages like Arabic and Hebrew and Urdu and right to left languages. And now we're in a hundred plus languages now and now we're really doubling down on the localization experience to make it feel truly local in every market around the world. (00:17:47): And so you can see how having these very big, audacious goals that you then just take a step after step towards helps then will it into existence or on every device. We started off obviously just with a web platform and then we launched our iPad app and then iPhone and then Android and then we spent years investing in cross-platform. So we have the same feature set across every device. And so you can see how these big amorphous things that seem very outlandish, you can then just will into existence after continual investment for a decade and it compounds over time.
turns.zh: 是的，太多了。我们的使命是赋予全球设计能力，我们将其分解为多个支柱任务。赋予每个人在任何设备上、用任何语言设计任何内容的能力，这听起来很复杂。但我们每年都会朝着这个使命设定阶段性目标。比如设计方面，起初专注于社交媒体、演示文稿、文档、网站、白板和视频。然后每年我们都会推出更多功能来实现“设计任何内容”的目标。在语言方面，我们从英语开始，然后是西班牙语，接着是20种语言，再到100种语言，再到阿拉伯语、希伯来语、乌尔都语等难学语言。现在我们支持100多种语言，并且正全力提升本地化体验，让全球每个市场都感受到真正的本土化。（00:17:47）你可以看到，设定这些宏大、雄心勃勃的目标，然后一步步推进，最终将其变为现实。比如设备覆盖方面，我们最初只有网页平台，后来推出了iPad应用、iPhone应用、安卓应用，接着花了数年时间投入跨平台开发。现在我们在所有设备上都提供相同的功能。你会发现，这些看似遥不可及的宏大构想，通过十年的持续投入，最终都能变为现实，而且随着时间推移，效果会越来越显著。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I see how all this is starting to fade together. There's this big crazy ambitious vision and below there are the mission pillars that are feeding into this vision and then the Crazy Big Goals within each of those mission pillars to measure your progress towards all these components of the mission.
turns.zh: 我发现这一切正逐渐融合在一起。有一个宏大而疯狂的远景目标，底层则有多个使命支柱为之注入动力，每个使命支柱下又设有“疯狂大目标”，以衡量你在这些使命组成要素上的进展。

turns.speaker: Melanie Perkins
turns.en: Exactly, exactly.
turns.zh: 没错，确实如此。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, so with all that in mind, there's also this kind of trade-off you have to make of just how ambitious you get because oftentimes sometimes maybe you never miss the goal, but many times people miss these very ambitious goals. How do you just find that balance between ambitious crazy but doable enough where people don't get discouraged?
turns.zh: 好的，考虑到这一点，你还得在目标的雄心壮志与可行性之间找到平衡点，因为有时人们可能达不到目标，但更多时候人们会错过这些极具挑战性的目标。如何在雄心勃勃又切实可行之间找到平衡，让人们不至于灰心丧气？

turns.speaker: Melanie Perkins
turns.en: I think with a crazy big goal, the thing we have been really great at is achieving them. The timeframe that we achieve them on has not always been very reliable. We have certainly not been able to have pin dart. What's it?
turns.zh: 我认为在设定疯狂大目标方面，我们一直很擅长实现它们。但实现的时间表并非始终可靠。我们当然无法做到精准到秒。是什么？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Bullseye?
turns.zh: 十环吗？

turns.speaker: Melanie Perkins
turns.en: We have not been very accurate with timing, but it's really interesting. I look back at a 2021 vision deck that we made obviously in 2021, but it was about 2026 and it was fascinating to see how much we'd actually been able to achieve from that vision deck and how many things were currently still in flight. And so by having that, I thought in 2021, some of those things may have happened a little quicker, but over the last five years they've really been coming into reality. And so we might think things are going to take six months and they take a year. We might think things are going to take six months and they take two years. This has been the case. We might think something's actually going to take our entire lifetime as some of those really truly Crazy Big Goals. And in fact, I don't even know if we can ever achieve them frankly. But they're such an important goal that even if you make a little step in their direction, they're worthwhile nonetheless.
turns.zh: 我们在时间把控上确实不够精准，但这很有意思。我回顾了2021年制定的愿景规划，显然是2021年制定的，但目标设定到2026年。看到我们从那份愿景规划中实际实现了那么多内容，而许多事项至今仍在推进中，这真的令人惊叹。因此，回想2021年，我曾以为有些目标可能会更快实现，但过去五年间它们确实逐渐成为现实。例如，我们原以为某些目标需要六个月就能达成，结果花了一年时间。有些目标我们以为需要六个月，最终却用了两年。现实就是如此。有些目标甚至可能需要我们终其一生去实现，比如那些真正疯狂的大目标。说实话，我甚至不确定我们能否实现它们。但这些目标如此重要，即便朝着目标迈出一小步，也绝对值得。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Whether you like him or not, Elon, this is similar to his, if you watch him, he sets these really ambitious goals and then often is far late on achieving them, but clearly it has worked out in achieving the crazy things that he's achieved. Something else I hear is you celebrate these goals in a really unique way. Talk about that.
turns.zh: 无论你喜不喜欢埃隆，如果你观察他，他也会设定这些极具雄心的目标，然后往往会延迟实现，但显然他实现了那些疯狂的目标。另外，我听说你们用一种独特的方式庆祝这些目标。能谈谈这方面吗？

turns.speaker: Melanie Perkins
turns.en: So when we have these Crazy Big Goals, we also have couple them with really fun celebrations. And so we attempt to make the Crazy Big Goals happen in a moment in time. So then when we achieve them, we actually have a really fun moment because if you're just trying to plod towards the top of the mountain always and you never take a little moment to pat yourself on the back, it would feel a little arduous. And so over the years we had all sorts of fun little celebrations where we have smashed great plates and released doves and had a La Tomatina festival. (00:20:51): All sorts of fun things just to take a moment with the team to celebrate that huge achievement. And so I think that you want to celebrate what you want to really focus on and what you want everyone to take that moment. So when you achieve that crazy big goal when we launch in Spanish, when we hit a hundred languages and then the so forth across the company, taking that moment to actually pat yourself on the back and pat the teams on the back and say, "Hey, we did this thing. That thing that seemed really hard, we've now achieved." And the mission is often each of the different mission pillars, they're obviously a long area of investment that's going to take a long time to get to, but being able to celebrate each of the rungs on that on the way there I think is extraordinarily important. And then everyone works extraordinarily hard to bring them to life and then it gives everyone a little moment to feel proud of themselves.
turns.zh: 因此，当我们设定这些疯狂的大目标时，我们也会为它们搭配一些非常有趣的庆祝活动。于是，我们试图在某个特定时刻让这些疯狂的大目标成为现实。这样，当我们实现目标时，就能享受到一个欢乐的时刻。如果你只是一直朝着山顶艰难攀登，却从不稍作停歇为自己喝彩，那过程会显得异常艰辛。多年来，我们策划了各种各样有趣的小庆典，比如摔碎大盘子、放飞鸽子、举办西红柿大战节。（00:20:51）：这些欢乐的时刻能让团队暂停脚步，共同庆祝这一重大成就。因此，我认为你需要庆祝那些你真正想关注的成果，让每个人都能抓住这一刻。当我们成功推出西班牙语版本、突破100种语言的里程碑，以及公司内其他类似的成就时，停下来为自己和团队击掌庆祝，说：“嘿，我们做到了。看似难以实现的目标，如今我们已经实现了。” 而公司的使命往往是各个不同的支柱任务，这些显然需要长期投入才能达成，但在实现目标的过程中，每一步的庆祝都显得格外重要。随后，每个人都会全力以赴将其变为现实，这也让每个人都有机会为自己的成就感到自豪。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It'd be very motivating to get to just break a bunch of plates. I really like that. Celebration strategy.
turns.zh: 能摔碎一堆盘子真是太有激励效果了。我真的很喜欢这个庆祝策略。

turns.speaker: Melanie Perkins
turns.en: We need to bring that one back. We haven't done that one in a while.
turns.zh: 我们得把这个传统带回来了。我们好久没这么做了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's a good one. I just love how concrete you're making this. So it's set these Crazy Big Goals, confine the component of the goals, set numbers there and then figure out the kind of steps you take to achieve these things. All fail is very easy. On the flip side of that, this is a segue. People hear these stories, they hear your story, they see Canva over the years and it's just this up into the right huge success story, one of the most successful companies in history. I imagine there have been many periods where things weren't going so great and when maybe things didn't look like they would work out. So let me just ask you this over the course of building Canva, once it started to click and started to feel like it was going to be a thing, was there a point where it started to again feel like, "Wow, maybe this may not work out. Maybe there's a huge setback that we may not get over?"
turns.zh: 这个主意不错。我喜欢你把这件事说得如此具体。所以先设定这些疯狂的大目标，拆解目标的各个组成部分，设定具体的数字，然后规划出实现这些目标的步骤。失败太容易了。另一方面，这是一个过渡话题。人们听了这些故事，听了你的故事，看了Canva这些年来的发展，它无疑是一个成功的典范，是历史上最成功的公司之一。我想在Canva的发展过程中，当一切开始步入正轨、感觉它即将成为一项大事业时，有没有某个时刻让你再次感到，“哇，也许这不会成功。也许会遇到无法克服的巨大挫折？”

turns.speaker: Melanie Perkins
turns.en: I think it's just a constant evolution. Every time the company doubles in size, pretty much all your systems break, all the things that were working don't work. A little example, in the early days we'd stand up and everyone would present their goals, what they're working on every day, every week. And then it kind of moved every month and then it was just taking too long because we've got so many people. And then it was sort of like we'd started doing these things called season openers and season openers were really fun where we got the entire company together, we talked about the goals that we'd achieved. And it was so funny because ahead of season openers, everyone would launch everything because they wanted to do it ahead of the season opener. And then we'd also set the goals for the coming cycle for the coming season at that point in time. (00:23:17): But then they started to become six hours long because we had so many people and so many teams. And so trying to find that right with the same philosophies of deep context for everyone with the same philosophies of the celebrations and the goals and trying to find that right flavor at every stage of scale is definitely hard. And so I think it's just a constant work in progress. Or back to your earlier point about timing of things, we were doing a front-end rewrite and we thought it would take about six months. It was really important because it was critical for cross-platform. It was critical for right to left. It was critical because we could only have five people working in our editor at any point in time because of the way the code base was structured and we thought it was going to take six months and then it took two years and it was two years of not shipping any product, two years of a product company not being able to ship product. (00:24:14): And that is such a core motivation for our team. He's shipping something, seeing great customer feedback and that kind of makes everyone feel happy and you've got momentum and it just felt like we're in a dark, dark tunnel that we could hardly see the end of the tunnel. And we didn't really know how long it was going to take because it just had to take as long as the tunnel was going to take. And it was a very hard time because other people would be launching this and that. And it was eventually we got out of that tunnel and it was extremely important that we did that work. We've now got two and a half thousand engineers and we're able to deliver amazing things that would've just been completely infeasible and simultaneous collaboration, so many things were baked into this. But yeah, it was not a fun period of time. A product company not shipping product is not really a recipe for fun.
turns.zh: 我觉得这就是一个持续演进的过程。每次公司规模翻倍时，几乎所有的系统都会崩溃，之前运作良好的东西也无法正常运行。举个小例子，早期我们会召开每周例会，所有人都会站起来汇报各自的目标和每周工作进展。后来这个汇报频率逐渐变为每月一次，但由于团队规模过大，这耗费了太多时间。于是我们开始举办“季开幕仪式”，这类活动非常有趣，全公司人员齐聚一堂，回顾已达成的目标。但在季开幕仪式前夕，每个人都会加班加点赶进度，只为能在仪式上展示成果。同时，我们也会在活动现场设定下一季度的目标。（00:23:17）但后来这种仪式持续时间长达六个小时——因为公司规模太大，团队过多。要在每个阶段都保持相同的深度上下文、庆祝仪式和目标设定，确实是个挑战。所以我觉得这就是一个持续改进的过程。或者回到你之前提到的时机问题——我们当时进行前端重写，原以为需要六个月。但这个项目至关重要，对跨平台支持至关重要，对左右排版至关重要。关键在于，由于代码库结构原因，编辑器同时只能有五个人工作，而这项工作本应在六个月内完成，结果拖了两年。这两年间，公司无法发布任何产品，整个团队陷入停滞。（00:24:14）这对我们团队来说是核心动力。当团队能交付成果，收获客户积极反馈时，每个人都会倍感振奋，形成良性循环。但当时我们就像身处黑暗隧道，看不到尽头，也不知道要走多久。周围其他公司都在不断推出新产品，而我们却深陷困境。最终我们走出困境，这项工作至关重要。如今我们拥有2500名工程师，能够实现以前不可想象的功能，例如同步协作等诸多创新。但那确实是一段艰难的时期。产品公司无法交付成果，绝非乐趣之源。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: For two years.
turns.zh: 整整两年。

turns.speaker: Melanie Perkins
turns.en: For two years.
turns.zh: 整整两年。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I feel like every builder listening to this knows exactly what you've been through and maybe not on that scale in those stakes, but you start on something, "Oh yeah, it'll take a few weeks," and then a year later you're still working on it.
turns.zh: 我觉得每个听众都能感同身受，或许规模和风险没那么大，但每个项目启动时都会说：“哦，几周就能完成。”结果一年后还在苦苦挣扎。

turns.speaker: Melanie Perkins
turns.en: Totally.
turns.zh: 完全正确。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Just was the mood really, I don't know, sad internally? Two years, that's a long time not to ship anything. Just what was it like internally during that period?
turns.zh: 当时大家情绪肯定很低落。两年时间不推出任何产品，时间太长了。那段时期公司内部是什么情况？

turns.speaker: Melanie Perkins
turns.en: I think it was kind of everything internally. We made it into a bit of a game. We had this game board and I bought these little rubber ducky sort of bath toys and we had, so we all the little components represented as a bath toy on this board and there was all these stages of went launched in product. There was an emergency lane at the end of it was home and hosed. And we did these weekly stand ups where everyone would come in and talk where their bath toy was at and just, we tried to make it fun for the team. So it was partly fun and it was partly distressing as all of our investors were like, "Hey, that thing." So I think it was both things at the same time. It was bonding let's say.
turns.zh: 我觉得这主要源于内部因素。我们把整个过程当成了一场游戏。我们设计了一个游戏板，还买了些橡胶鸭子之类的玩具浴具，把所有产品开发阶段都用这些玩具浴具来具象化。游戏板的最后是"紧急通道"，象征着产品上线后的挑战。我们每周都会开例会，每个人都要汇报自己的进展，努力让整个团队充满乐趣。所以这既有趣味性，又充满焦虑感——毕竟我们的投资者总会说：“嘿，这个产品。”所以我觉得这两种情绪交织在一起。可以说，这段经历增进了团队凝聚力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. Speaking of investors, speaking of other hard times, there's a very famous story about Canva. Early on you pitched over a hundred investors and over a hundred investors said no to you when you were just starting Canva. I think that's important. The investors than any founder I've talked to actually tries to pitch. It's impressive you tried that hard and went for so many pitches and finally got someone to take a bet. Now you are something like a $40 billion company making 3.3 billion ARR. I think there's something like $240 million monthly active users, one of the hottest private companies in the world. Just how does this feel?
turns.zh: 好的。说到投资者，再谈谈其他艰难时期，Canva有个著名的故事。早期创业时，Canva向一百多个投资者推销产品，但几乎所有人都拒绝了。我认为这很重要。与我交谈过的创始人相比，Canva的投资者确实更愿意尝试。你们能坚持不懈地多次推销，最终找到愿意投资的人，这令人钦佩。如今Canva估值400亿美元，年营收达33亿美元，月活用户约2.4亿，成为全球最热门的私营公司之一。这种感觉如何？

turns.speaker: Melanie Perkins
turns.en: I don't know. It was really clear in my mind that it was the future and I thought the investors were wrong, frankly. But investors also gave really helpful feedback and feedback often in the form of rejection. So they would say, "Oh, your market's not big enough." And I would say, "It's going to be huge." And I'd add a new page in my pitch deck that said how big the market I believe was. And then they'd say, "You're the same as some other company," coupled with rejection, and I would say, "Hey, now I've got a new slide in my pitch deck that shows all the players and the huge gap in the market that we believe we're going to fill." Or most investors just knew absolutely nothing about design or the industry that we're in. And so we then ended up with the first few slides saying, "Here's the lay of the land today. Here's the problem that we're going to solve." (00:27:53): And so while it was extraordinarily frustrating, their feedback made us stronger and made our pitch deck stronger. And it was sort of from that chaos to clarity. At the start it was this idea and then through the copious amounts of rejection, the pitch deck got stronger and more refined. So then when people, the first time I remember I spoke to someone for hours and they eventually got it. They were really committed to understanding what we were trying to do, but then not everyone has six hours to understand a concept. And so being able to take all the gems of wisdom from that conversation and have that understood really clearly in a really short period of time and have all of the reasons that people were rejecting us pre-answered in that initial pitch deck was really important. And I think that's probably one of the reasons why when I look back at our 2012 pitch deck, it's so valid and really still captures what we're doing today. And so I think that rejection in some ways makes you stronger if you can persist through.
turns.zh: 我不知道。当时我坚信这是未来的趋势，坦白说，我认为投资者错了。但投资者也提供了很有价值的反馈，尽管往往以拒绝的形式出现。比如他们会说：“你的市场规模不够大。”我会说：“它会变得非常大。”然后我在演示文稿中添加新页面，展示我认为市场规模有多大。接着他们会说：“你和其他公司太像了。”伴随着拒绝，我会说：“嘿，我在演示文稿中新增了一页，展示所有市场参与者以及我们认为能填补的巨大市场空白。”大多数投资者对设计或我们所在的行业一无所知。所以最初的几页幻灯片会说：“当下行业现状如何？我们要解决什么问题？” （00:27:53）虽然过程极其令人沮丧，但他们的反馈让我们更强大，也让演示文稿更完善。从混乱到清晰。最初只是一个想法，经过无数次拒绝后，演示文稿逐渐完善。直到第一次有人花了几个小时听我讲解，最终终于理解。他们真的致力于理解我们的目标，但并非每个人都有六个小时来理解一个概念。因此，能从那次对话中提取所有智慧精华，并在极短时间内清晰传达，让人们预先理解拒绝我们的原因，这非常重要。我认为这可能就是为什么回看2012年的演示文稿时，它依然有效，至今仍准确概括了我们正在做的事情。所以我认为，只要坚持下去，拒绝反倒能让你更强大。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Well, I think beyond that, I've never heard this part of the story. It's not just persisting, it's actually iterating and taking feedback that you're hearing to continue to evolve the pitch to a place where, "Okay, I finally get what you're doing." That is such a cool part of the story. How much of that vision and product changed throughout that journey versus just the way you pitched it and convinced people?
turns.zh: 嗯，我觉得除此之外，我从未听过这个故事的这部分内容。这不只是坚持不懈，更是不断迭代并根据反馈调整方案，持续完善提案，最终让对方感叹“终于明白你们在做什么了”。这真是故事中最精彩的部分。在整个过程中，愿景和产品发生了多大的变化？与你最初的提案相比，又有怎样的不同？

turns.speaker: Melanie Perkins
turns.en: It was pretty consistent, but the way we articulated it changed greatly. And so for example, I wouldn't, in the early days, articulate the problem very much. And I went into, "Here's the cool solution." And so then the first few pages became very much more problem-based because if people don't understand the problem then they can't understand or care about your solution. And so there was a lot of refinement on the way it was articulated, but the actual vision itself I think was pretty consistent through.
turns.zh: 变化不大，但表达方式却大不相同。比如，早期我不太会详细阐述问题，而是直接抛出“这里有个很酷的解决方案”。后来，前几页内容变得更侧重于问题分析，因为如果人们不理解问题，就无法理解或关注你的解决方案。因此，表达方式经过了多次优化，但核心愿景始终如一。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Guessing a lot of founders ask for your advice on raising money, getting started, having gone through so much rejection early on. What's your general advice to folks that are having a hard time fundraising?
turns.zh: 我猜很多创业者会向你请教融资建议、创业初期如何应对多次拒绝等问题。对于那些融资困难的人，你有什么通用建议？

turns.speaker: Melanie Perkins
turns.en: I mean, I can only go on my experience, but I think it's sort of the dark tunnel analogy. Or chaos to clarity, let's go with that one. It's a slightly friendlier analogy and I think just taking the rejection and turning into things that you can control. So I can control my pitch deck, I can control the number of people I'm speaking to and I just spoke to literally everyone. And I think that continuing to use it to refine it rather than taking it as a personal rejection, I think it's really important to think how can I improve? How can I help someone to understand it? Some people are never going to understand it. I remember pitching an investor that had the lean startup book behind them when I was pitching them and they were never going to like Canva. We were not the lean startup. That was not the way that we were approaching it whatsoever. So there's some people that are just going to never like you and that's okay. I think it's important to find some people that do what you're trying to say and trying to do and kind of finding your tribe, I think.
turns.zh: 我只能根据自身经验谈谈。用黑暗隧道的比喻比较贴切，或者用从混乱到清晰的转变来形容。后者更易于理解，我认为关键在于将拒绝转化为可控因素。比如，我可以优化演示文稿，调整沟通对象，我几乎把所有人都联系了一遍。关键是持续改进，而不是把拒绝视为个人失败。思考如何改进、如何让对方理解很重要。有些人永远无法理解你，但这没关系。记得我向一位投资者推销 Canva 时，他们对精益创业理念深信不疑，但根本不喜欢 Canva。我们根本不是精益创业模式。有些人注定不喜欢你，但这没关系。重要的是找到认同你的理念和方向的人，形成自己的团队。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: As an investor, this is really interesting to hear because it tells you there are companies like Canva there that everyone's turning down, a hundred investors passed on, that you might still be able to invest in. (00:30:58): Talking about your growth as a leader, say if you compare Melanie of today to Melanie of, I don't know, 12, 13 years ago when you were just starting Canva, what would you say is most different in terms of leadership?
turns.zh: 作为投资者，听你讲这些很有启发。这表明像 Canva 这样的公司可能被无数投资者拒绝，但你或许仍能投资。（00:30:58）谈谈你作为领导者的成长。若将今天的梅兰妮与 12 年前刚创立 Canva 时的梅兰妮相比，领导力方面最大的变化是什么？

turns.speaker: Melanie Perkins
turns.en: I don't really know. Probably if you ask other people around me, they'd probably be more observant. But it is funny because there's some things that I think that I need to change and then I realize you go into it the same as some other company. And sometimes we even try that for a while and then we try that out and we're like... It didn't really work for us. And it's kind of building a house that you want every brick in the house to match. And if you go and try and take some bricks from someone else's house and stick it in your house, it's probably going to not look very matched. And so trying to find things that are authentic to us and are authentic to everything that's come before it, is just that constant, constant thing. And then each scale of each stage of scale of the company rather than going, taking someone else's bricks and trying to stick that in your house, trying to build the thing that's authentic. (00:31:59): So I think there's many things that are the same, but obviously the stage and scale and we're constantly having to give away hats. And so you kind of think about it in the very early days. We just a few of us, two of us in Fusion and then three of us in a little tiny group, and you kind of wear a hundred hats and then you have to be able to give away those hats to other people that can then do that way better than yourself. And so I'm sure there's been a few skills I guess I would've had to have developed over the last decade to be able to give away those hats. But yeah, I think there's a lot of things that we've had to do and double down on that was more authentic to the way we did it in the early days actually.
turns.zh: 我真不太清楚。或许你要是问我身边的人，他们可能更善于观察。但说起来挺有趣的，有些事情我觉得自己需要改进，结果却发现其他公司也在这么做。有时我们甚至尝试了一阵子，结果发现根本行不通。这就像盖房子时想让每块砖都完美契合，但如果从别人家拿来砖块拼凑进自己的房子，效果肯定不理想。所以，要找到真正适合我们、也契合前人经验的东西，这是一项永无止境的工作。每个阶段、每个规模的公司都面临着这样的挑战——与其照搬别人家的模式，不如专注于打造真正属于自己的东西。（00:31:59）：我觉得很多事情都是相通的，但显然随着公司规模和阶段的变化，我们不得不不断让渡权力。早期创业时，我们只有几个人——Fusion部门两人组，另外三个人组成了一个小团队——每个人都要身兼数职，后来不得不把这些职责交给比我们更擅长的人。我相信过去十年里我不得不培养的很多技能，就是为了能把这些职责顺利移交出去。是的，我认为我们必须反复回归初心，坚守那些早期成功的秘诀。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that story. I think again, if anyone working at a company that has gone through a lot of growth has experienced that when people from other companies come in and, "Here's how we did it at this company." Is there an example of some there that just like, "Here's something that this company brought in and people from this company thought we should do and we try it and didn't work?"
turns.zh: 我特别喜欢这个故事。我想，任何经历过快速发展期的公司员工，肯定都遇到过这种情况——其他公司的人进来后说：“我们公司是这么做的。”有没有例子，比如某个公司引入的方案，结果团队觉得不合适，尝试后却失败了？

turns.speaker: Melanie Perkins
turns.en: I won't go into specific examples, but so many times over. And I think that, I mean maybe that's probably, in answer your other question, we did things our way because that was the only way we knew. And there was many, many times over the years that we didn't have confidence in the way we were doing things and we were like, "Oh, they've done it from a big company that's bigger than our company. Let's go do that." And that hasn't always worked out so well for us. And so yeah, I think confidence in how we take what is authentic to us and do it at the next level of scale is a constant work in progress. It feels like, as I was saying before, systems break and need to be reinvented but also reimagined for that next layer of scale rather than going to try to get something off the shelf from another company.
turns.zh: 我不会举具体例子，但这种情况太多次了。我想，或许这就是为什么我们坚持自己的方式，因为这是我们唯一熟悉的路径。这些年来，我们很多次对现有做法缺乏信心，比如“哦，某个大公司这么做过，我们也应该效仿”。但结果并不理想。所以是的，我认为要在新阶段、更大规模上保持初心，是一项持续的挑战。就像我之前说的，系统会崩溃，需要重建和重新构想，以适应更高层次的规模，而不是照搬其他公司的现成方案。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I imagine it also helped that you were in Australia away from the Bay Area and where all these other big companies are at, just being able to do it your own way.
turns.zh: 我猜在澳大利亚远离湾区和其他大公司聚集地，也能让你们专心走自己的路，这对你们帮助很大。

turns.speaker: Melanie Perkins
turns.en: Yeah, very much so.
turns.zh: 是的，确实如此。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Did you know that I have a whole team that helps me with my podcast and with my newsletter? I want everyone on that team to be super happy and thrive in the roles. JustWorks knows that your employees are more than just your employees, they're your people. My team is spread out across Colorado, Australia, Nepal, West Africa and San Francisco. My life would be so incredibly complicated to hire people internationally to pay people on time and in their local currencies and to answer their HR questions 24/7. But with JustWorks, it's super easy whether you're setting up your own automated payroll, offering premium benefits or hiring internationally. JustWorks offer simple software and 24 7 human support from small business experts for you and your people. They do your human resources so that you can do right by your people, JustWorks, for your people. (00:34:38): Is there anything else that is a good example of how you did something pretty different from how other companies operate? Anything else that comes to mind as a fun example?
turns.zh:
你们知道吗，我有一个完整的团队来协助我制作播客和处理通讯事务。我希望团队中的每个人都能快乐工作，胜任各自的角色。JustWorks 深知员工不只是普通雇员，他们是团队中不可或缺的成员。我的团队成员遍布科罗拉多州、澳大利亚、尼泊尔、西非和旧金山。若要在全球范围内招聘员工、按当地货币准时支付薪资、全天候解答员工的人力资源问题，这无疑会让我的生活变得异常复杂。但有了 JustWorks，一切都变得轻而易举——无论是建立自动化薪资系统、提供优质福利，还是进行跨国招聘。JustWorks 为您和您的团队提供简单易用的软件及全天候的人力资源支持服务，让您能真正为员工着想。这就是 JustWorks，为员工而生。

（00:34:38）：还有其他能很好地说明你们与其他公司运营方式截然不同的例子吗？能想到的有趣案例是什么？

turns.speaker: Melanie Perkins
turns.en: The goal driven structure, I think the things that we were talking about before. So the mission, actually breaking that down into the mission pillars, breaking those mission pillars down into the goals that we're then pursuing and then celebrating those goals when we do achieve them, I think is a deeply underloved way of building a company. Often people have a mission that's kind of on the wall somewhere and then what they're actually doing and the way they actually make money and the way people actually spend their time is in a very, very different direction from that original mission. And I think the magic is when you can bring those two things together and so you can have your mission, you can have your mission pillars that actually are helping to achieve that. And I think there's a real authenticity in that for customers as well, is that you are actually doing the thing that you promised you do, and it all ladders up together. It's certainly not an easy way to run a company, but I think that when you do get that formula, I think that there's a lot of authenticity with what you're saying you're doing, you're actually doing.
turns.zh: 我认为目标驱动型架构很重要，就是我们之前讨论的那些内容。比如使命宣言，拆解成使命支柱，再细化为具体目标，达成目标后进行庆祝——这是一种被严重低估的企业管理方式。很多公司挂着使命宣言，却在实际运营中偏离轨道，比如赚钱方式与初衷背道而驰，员工时间分配与目标不符。关键在于将两者统一起来，让使命宣言真正落地。这样既能让客户感受到真诚，又能确保言行一致。这种管理模式确实不易，但一旦找到正确的公式，言行一致就会自然而然。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to come back to that. That's a whole really cool process. Do you have with closing the loop with customers, but something else I want to talk about while we're in this topic of growth over time. I saw you post something about how you had to realize they had to slow down and not just work, work, work like crazy. Talk about just that realization and why that ended up being so valuable.
turns.zh: 我想再谈谈这个问题。闭环管理客户的流程很棒。但在谈论长期发展时，我还想聊聊别的话题。我看到你发帖说必须意识到要放慢脚步，不能疯狂加班。能谈谈这个认识转变吗？为什么它如此重要？

turns.speaker: Melanie Perkins
turns.en: So in the early days, I would just work seven days a week round the clock. In our very first company, we actually had printing presses because we were printing the yearbooks in my mom's house and then delivering them to schools around Australia. And in the early days of Canva, we certainly were working all weekend, all hours of the day. It was just constant. But when you've been doing this for a while, if you just keep working at that pace, I don't think it's good for anyone's health, mental health or anything else. So I think finding ways to continue, I still work extraordinarily hard, but to continue to have that balance in my day to day where I actually go to sleep, I find time to do things like going for walks or doing yoga, journaling I find extraordinarily helpful to make sure that I can always bring my best to everything that I'm doing.
turns.zh: 早期的时候，我每周七天无休地工作。我们最初的公司实际上有印刷机，因为我们在妈妈家印制年册，然后分发到澳大利亚各地的学校。在Canva的初期阶段，我们确实整个周末都在工作，几乎全天候投入工作。这种状态持续不断。但当你长期处于这种工作节奏中，无论是对健康、心理健康还是其他方面都不利。所以我认为，要想继续前进，我仍然会非常努力地工作，但同时也要保持日常生活的平衡——比如睡个好觉、散散步、做做瑜伽、写写日记——这些对我来说都非常有帮助，能确保我始终能在工作中发挥出最佳状态。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's easy to say that kind of stuff. It must be really hard to actually make time for that thing. Is there anything for those sorts of things, is there anything that you do that allows you to actually protect that time to actually do these things? Because as you said, there's a billion things that are just looking for your attention constantly.
turns.zh: 说起来容易，做起来肯定很难。您有没有什么方法能确保为这些事情腾出时间？正如您所说，总有无数的事情不断吸引我们的注意力。

turns.speaker: Melanie Perkins
turns.en: I feel like I've developed some healthy habits over the years. I don't have emails on my phone and so when I shut my laptop, I actually tune out and then if there's a real issue, I'll get an emergency call or page. But I think trying to delineate I think is really important. So when I'm working, I'm all in and then when I'm not working, I'm all out. And actually giving that mental space I think is really important. I've spoken to a lot of founders that haven't quite found that and then do struggle with it. So when they're working every weekend it feels like the right thing, but then sometimes you can miss the forest from the trees when you're just working harder and harder, but maybe you're actually working on the wrong thing. And so I think being able to step away a little just to be able to get perspective is actually really beneficial.
turns.zh: 这些年我养成了些健康的习惯。我手机里没有邮箱，所以当我关上笔记本电脑时，就能真正放松下来。当然，如果有紧急情况，我会接到紧急电话或通知。但我认为划分界限真的很重要。工作时全心投入，休息时全身心放松。给自己留出这样的心理空间非常重要。我接触过很多创始人，他们没能做到这一点，结果深受其害。他们觉得每个周末工作是理所当然的，但有时因为埋头于工作而顾此失彼，可能会错失大局。所以我认为偶尔抽身出来，换个视角，真的很有益处。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to come back to this closing the loop process. Let's say that you have where you figure out what to build. A lot of your ideas come actually from the community. Talk about just that process and how many of your ideas actually came from your community.
turns.zh: 我想再谈谈闭环流程。假设你已经确定了要开发的产品。很多想法其实都来自社区。能否谈谈这个过程，以及有多少想法是来自社区的？

turns.speaker: Melanie Perkins
turns.en: Oh, it's one of my favorite things. We've been doing it for years now, and so we get more than a million requests from our community every year and we've got a whole incredible team that then tallies them, breaks them down, and then delivers them to all of our product teams and then those actually get closed. So this year we've closed more than 200 loops, but we know that each one of those things is going to be loved and needed by so many more people that don't bother to actually fill out the request form. So many things from gradient text, like little things like gradient text to really big things like our Sheets product. There's just been countless products. In the early days with our AI products, we didn't release them to teachers because we knew there was a lot of hesitancy for teachers using AI in the classroom. (00:39:03): And we got so many requests from teachers saying, "Can I please use this MagicWrite in the classroom?" And so with them we unlocked that and put on safety controls for teachers. And so it's just constant, actually. It's just part of our product process. I think there's two parts to product. One is building the future and towards the mission and the mission pillars as I was saying before. And the other is actually listening to our community and building what they want. And so I think that that's the two core pieces of product in my mind. And the closing the loop comes in so many different forms. There's the explicit asks, and then the other thing that we double down on all the time is user testing and watching people use it. And if people hesitate clicking a button or people don't quite understand how something works, it's amazing to me how you can find 10 random people on the internet and they can give such astute feedback that then is so representative for such a large number of people. I've personally run hundreds if not thousands of user tests myself and it's been deeply embedded in our product teams also.
turns.zh: 哦，这是我最喜欢做的事情之一。我们已经这样做了很多年，每年都会收到社区提交的超过一百万条请求。我们有一支非常出色的团队负责整理这些请求，进行分类，然后将它们分发给各个产品团队，最终这些请求都会被落实。今年我们已经完成了200多个需求闭环，但我们知道，还有更多没有填写请求表格的人会喜欢并需要这些功能。从渐变文字这样的小改进，到像Sheets产品这样的大型功能，数不胜数的产品都源于此。在人工智能产品早期阶段，我们没有向教师开放这些产品，因为我们知道教师在课堂上使用AI存在诸多顾虑。（00:39:03）：但我们收到了很多教师的请求，他们说：“我能在课堂上使用MagicWrite吗？”于是我们为教师解锁了这一功能，并为他们设置了安全控制措施。实际上，这是一个持续的过程，是我们产品开发流程的组成部分。在我看来，产品开发有两个核心部分：一是构建未来，朝着使命和核心价值观前进；二是倾听用户需求，打造他们真正想要的产品。在我看来，闭环反馈有两种形式：一种是用户明确提出的需求；另一种是我们始终重视的用户测试和观察用户使用行为。如果用户在点击按钮时犹豫不决，或者不理解某项功能的工作原理，那么我惊讶地发现，随便在网上找10个用户就能获得极具代表性的深刻反馈。就我个人而言，我亲自进行了数百次甚至数千次用户测试，这一做法也已深深融入我们的产品团队。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow, that must be really stressful for someone looking at a test of Canva, trying to try something when you're in the room.
turns.zh: 哇，如果有人在测试Canva时，想尝试某个功能，而你又在现场观看，这肯定压力很大。

turns.speaker: Melanie Perkins
turns.en: It's actually, we do it all online actually. I mean the ones I've run are typically online. So people are so much more frank I think when it's just them and their camera and they don't really... Yeah, they tell you really how it is.
turns.zh: 实际上我们全程在线进行测试。我参与过的测试通常都是在线的。我觉得当用户只需面对摄像头时，他们会更加坦诚，不会有所顾忌……是的，他们会如实反馈问题，这对大量用户来说极具参考价值。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there a tool or a kind of a process there that you find really helpful? I don't know if you want to name names of products or anything like that, but it's something that you find helpful or useful.
turns.zh: 有没有什么工具或流程对你们特别有帮助？我不知道你是否想提及具体产品名称，但肯定有对你有用的东西。

turns.speaker: Melanie Perkins
turns.en: Yeah, we use a lot of UserTesting.com, find that super valuable.
turns.zh: 是的，我们大量使用UserTesting.com，觉得它非常有价值。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: All right, go user testing. Okay. Something else that I know is really important to you and also really unique to Canva is something that's called the two-step plan. You mentioned this earlier, I want to definitely talk about this. What is the two-step plan? Why is this so important to you?
turns.zh: 好的，去进行用户测试吧。好的。我知道还有一件事对你们非常重要，也是Canva的独特之处，那就是所谓的两步计划。你之前提过这个，我一定要深入探讨一下。什么是两步计划？为什么它对你如此重要？

turns.speaker: Melanie Perkins
turns.en: Yeah, so when you were asking about Crazy Big Goals, I think this is our most macro, most crazy biggest goal. Step one, build one of the world's most valuable companies and step two, do the most good we can do. And in our early days I thought I'd do step one and then step two and realize that actually step one can fuel step two and step two can fuel step one. And so that's been a really big part of Canva for some years now. In the early days we took the 1% pledge, which I think is an incredible program. Every single person, every single company should take that where you give 1% of time, money, equity and profitability. And I think that's a really easy thing to do in the early days that then can compound greatly over time. We also knew that Canva's equity was obviously going to be a really key part of it. (00:41:35): So Cliff and I owned a little over 30% of Canva, and so we decided we were going to take 30% of Canva and use it to do the most good we can do. And we are doing that. So we're doing all of our donating through the Canva Foundation. We've just, over the last few years, we've donated $50 million to GiveDirectly, where they give money directly to people in Malawi who are in extreme poverty and then they can use that money on their family to go to school, to get healthcare, to start small businesses, to get a roof so they can sleep in without being wet. Just real truly basic human needs things. And we've just announced that we're going to be giving another a hundred million dollars over the next four years to people in extreme poverty. And it's just like when you go and sit with people and you hear about how they're spending, what's very microscopic amount at $550 doesn't buy us that much, but it's a life-changing amount of money for people in extreme poverty and it's truly transformational what it can do. (00:42:39): And you meet people and you hear their stories and it's truly the best money I could ever imagine spending. And that crazy big dream I was mentioning earlier of everyone having basic human needs met, it's so completely insane that isn't the case today. There's no specific reason why people don't have their basic human needs met on our planet, but we just haven't got to act together as humanity. And so that is a truly crazy, big dream. But back to the two-step plan. Step one, build one of the world's most valuable companies and step two do the most good we can do. And finding ways to do that at the same time I think is extraordinarily important.
turns.zh: 是啊，所以当你问起"疯狂的宏伟目标"时，我觉得这就是我们最宏大、最疯狂的终极目标。第一步，打造全球最具价值的公司；第二步，尽最大努力去造福世界。在公司初期，我以为自己会先完成第一步，再处理第二步，但后来发现第一步能为第二步提供动能，反之亦然。多年来，这一直是 Canva 的重要理念。早期我们参与了"1%承诺"项目，我认为这是一个极其了不起的倡议。每个人，每家公司都应该践行这项承诺——拿出1%的时间、金钱、股权和利润去帮助他人。尤其在公司初期阶段，这看似简单易行，但随着时间推移，其影响力会呈指数级增长。我们深知 Canva 的股权将是实现这一目标的关键。（00:41:35）所以我和克里夫持有公司超过30%的股权，决定将这部分股权用于最大限度地造福社会。目前所有捐赠都通过 Canva基金会进行。过去几年，我们已向GiveDirectly捐赠5000万美元，该机构直接将资金发放给马拉维极端贫困人群，帮助他们用于子女教育、医疗保健、创业发展、建造住所等基本生活需求。最近我们宣布未来四年将再向极端贫困人群捐赠1亿美元。与这些人交流时，你会发现即使是微不足道的5美元对我们来说不算什么，但对极端贫困人群而言却能改变命运，带来翻天覆地的变化。（00:42:39）当你聆听他们的故事时，会深切体会到这是最值得花费的善款。早前提到的"让每个人都能满足基本生活需求"这个疯狂宏伟的梦想，在当今世界看来依然遥不可及。地球上不存在无法满足基本生活需求的人群，这绝非客观原因，而是人类尚未携手行动。正因如此，这个梦想才显得格外疯狂。但回到两步计划：第一步，打造全球最具价值的公司；第二步，尽最大努力造福世界。在我看来，找到两者协同的路径至关重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's incredible. It makes me think about, not to mention Elon again, but Elon's three-step strategy plan and it's like build better cars versus this is like, "Okay, solve all the problems of the world and make the world a better place." What a better master plan to compare. Something else about this that I love is a lot of companies have this, have something philanthropic going on with the company and it's like sitting in a doc on some page. It's part of their mission. It's not actually that big of a deal to them. What I hear from folks at Canva is something you talk about all the time. This is an actually core part of how you work and think and how you set goals and set vision and missions.
turns.zh: 这太了不起了。这让我不禁联想到——当然不是拿埃隆来做比较——但埃隆的三步战略规划，比如"打造更优质的汽车"和"解决世界所有问题，让世界变得更美好"相比，这无疑是更宏大的蓝图。还有一点让我深受触动的是，许多公司只是把慈善事业挂在嘴边，写进公司使命宣言，但实际上并未投入太多真心。而在 Canva，人们谈论最多的是这项事业，它已然融入了公司运营的方方面面，是真正指导人们工作与决策的核心价值。

turns.speaker: Melanie Perkins
turns.en: Yeah, I'm happy to hear that. I wouldn't do Canva if it wasn't going to have a positive impact on the world. For me, getting really rich is not a goal unto itself whatsoever. It's a means to an end and I've been very blessed to be able to do some work and that creates wealth that can then go and have people's basic human needs met. But they're working just as hard, but they don't have the opportunity. And even our education product, it's now used by a hundred million people each month and we are in most school districts and rolled out across countries and being able to bring quality education tools to every, and we give that away for free as well. Being able to help empower schools all around the world and we're going to be doubling down and doubling down into that product to bring quality education to all. I think it gives so much more meaning behind work. We've also, between our education product and our non-profit program where we also give away our paid product for free, we are giving away 1.5 billion of product a year now. And so the impact that that can have and the ripple effect of that I think is pretty great. And I think for all of us, it gives a lot more meaning to our work than, "Get Rich."
turns.zh: 是啊，很高兴听到你这么说。如果Canva不能对世界产生积极影响，我是不会做这个项目的。对我来说，赚大钱本身并不是目标，而是达成某个目的的手段。我很幸运能从事一些工作，这些工作能创造财富，进而满足人们的基本需求。但有些人同样努力工作，却没有这样的机会。就拿我们的教育产品来说，现在每月有1亿人使用，我们的系统已覆盖多数学区，并在全球推广，致力于为每个人提供优质教育工具，而且这些工具都是免费提供的。我们正全力以赴推进这项产品，让优质教育触手可及。我认为这为工作赋予了更深层的意义。再加上我们的教育产品和非营利项目（我们将付费产品免费赠送），现在每年免费赠送的工具已达15亿份。其产生的积极影响和连锁反应，我认为是相当惊人的。对我们所有人而言，这比"赚大钱"更有意义。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. So speaking of product, coming back to that, you guys are launching something, maybe you've already launched it by the time this comes out, what I heard described as the biggest launching canvas history, no big deal, that's a high bar. Considering all the things you guys have launched, what are you launching? Why is it such a big deal?
turns.zh: 好的，说到产品，回到正题，你们即将推出新产品，也许在本访谈播出时已经上线了。据我所知，这是Canva史上最大规模的发布，没什么大不了的，这标准挺高的。考虑到你们推出的众多产品，这次发布的重点是什么？为什么意义重大？

turns.speaker: Melanie Perkins
turns.en: We are extraordinarily excited about what we are launching. I guess the whole mission of Canva is to empower the world to design. And so what has been enabled by new technology with all of AI has been just really profound. Enabling people to take their idea and turn it into design a design and have as little friction between those two points. So we are doubling down radically on our video product and bring some incredible capabilities to our mobile and desktop platform. We are launching email, which has been one of our most hotly requested features from enterprise customers around the world and business customers around the world who want to be able to design with Canva's drag and drop ease and to be able to create an email. We are launching forms, we are launching, probably one of the most exciting things is the way we're embedding AI across the entire product suite. (00:46:12): And so you can actually use AI to design a presentation, a video, a email, a website. All of these things can actually now be done inside the core editor, inside the design tab, which is used by 170. It's used 170 million times a month. And then on our elements tab, which is used 900 million times a month, we are also embedding AI. So you can actually generate a video, you can generate a canvas code and you can generate photos all directly inside that platform. And then we're also launching comments as lots of our customers use Canvas to comment and collaborate. And now you can actually just tag at Canvas and you can collaborate. You can just say, "Hey, can you make this title shorter? Can you do this? Can you do that?" And it has all of the context of the design so in situ, you can actually just have a collaborator that can help get your work done. So we are pretty excited about all of this.
turns.zh: 我们对即将推出的产品充满期待。Canva的使命是赋能全球设计力量。借助AI新技术带来的变革，让人们能更轻松地将创意转化为设计，这意义非凡。我们将大力投入视频产品，赋予移动端和桌面端平台更强功能。我们推出的邮件功能，是全球企业和商业客户最热切期待的功能之一，他们希望能借助Canva的拖放式操作轻松设计邮件。我们还将推出表单功能，嵌入AI技术的创新之处尤为令人兴奋。（00:46:12）用户现在可以在核心编辑器（每月使用1.7亿次）和元素库（每月使用9亿次）中直接运用AI技术设计演示文稿、视频、邮件和网站。评论功能也将上线，目前许多用户通过Canva进行评论与协作。现在用户可以在Canva上直接标注需求，实时协作，比如“标题能不能更简洁？能不能调整这个？能不能改那个？”所有设计细节都保留原样，协作者可以即时提供帮助。我们对这些创新成果充满期待。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. Something I'm going to just let people know, I don't know if people know all this, how many products you all have now. I think a lot of people think of Canva as a design graphics for social media and marketing and things like that, but you also have spreadsheets, docs, whiteboards, charts, code, AI coding tool. And now what I'm hearing is email forums. There's probably a few other things I'm not thinking [inaudible 00:47:36]-
turns.zh: 太棒了。我得跟大家说一下，我不知道大家是否都了解，你们现在有多少产品了。很多人以为 Canva 只是用于社交媒体和营销设计图之类的，但其实你们还有电子表格、文档、白板、图表、代码、AI 编码工具。现在我听说还有邮件论坛。可能还有些我没想起来的东西[00:47:36不可听清] -

turns.speaker: Melanie Perkins
turns.en: Yeah, truly design anything. We're literally living up to that.
turns.zh: 是啊，真的是能设计任何东西。我们确实在践行这个理念。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh my god, it's happening.
turns.zh: 天哪，这真的实现了。

turns.speaker: Melanie Perkins
turns.en: 100 million people design a presentation in Canva each month now and it's pretty fascinating to see that when you speak to, I saw a tweet some time ago. They were talking about how it's a generational thing that a certain generation uses Microsoft, a certain generation uses Google. Gen Z, the way they design a presentation is in Canva, but it's not just generational for those with other generational ilk, but it is been fascinating to see that come to life.
turns.zh: 现在每月有1亿人用Canva设计演示文稿，这太令人惊叹了。我之前看到一条推文，提到某代人用微软，另一代人用谷歌，而Z世代用Canva设计演示文稿。但这不只是代际差异，看到这样的成果真的很棒。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The email product, is that like a email client product or It's a design emails that you can then send through your products?
turns.zh: 邮件产品是邮件客户端产品，还是可以设计邮件然后通过你们的产品发送的邮件设计工具？

turns.speaker: Melanie Perkins
turns.en: It is design emails, so you can design email, then you can take that code and you can pop it into any email platform that you use.
turns.zh: 是邮件设计工具，所以你可以设计邮件，然后把代码插入任何你使用的邮件平台。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: How do you think about products you're going to expand to, I know there's trade secrets here. You don't want to tell everyone where you're going next, but just how do you approach, here's where we're going next.
turns.zh: 你们接下来的产品扩展方向是怎样的？我知道这涉及商业机密，你们不想透露下一步的方向，但能不能谈谈你们的规划，接下来要往哪儿发展？

turns.speaker: Melanie Perkins
turns.en: So our mission, empower world design, empower everyone to design anything with every ingredient in every language on every device, and just take those things very literally. So to literally design anything, to literally publish anywhere. And so we now print in 50 something countries around the world and you can get it printed and delivered to your house. And we plant it.
turns.zh: 我们的使命是赋能全球设计，让每个人都能用任何语言、在任何设备上设计任何内容。这句话要字面理解。所以是真正能设计任何东西，能真正发布到任何地方。现在我们在全球50多个国家提供打印服务，你可以下单打印并送货上门。我们还提供种植服务。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I actually did that, while you're on it.
turns.zh: 我刚好做过这个，你提起来的时候。

turns.speaker: Melanie Perkins
turns.en: Oh, awesome.
turns.zh: 太棒了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I wasn't planning this, but I had a print thing delivered to my house. It's so cool.
turns.zh: 我本来没打算做这个，但家里收到了打印件，太酷了。

turns.speaker: Melanie Perkins
turns.en: Oh, yeah. Exactly.
turns.zh: 对啊，就是这样。点击打印，东西就会包装精美地送到你家门口。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: We have to go to a print shop in this freaking graphic and well here's a button. Let's click that.
turns.zh: 没错。点击打印就行，结果效果超棒。

turns.speaker: Melanie Perkins
turns.en: Exactly. Just click print and it pops up beautifully packaged to your door.
turns.zh: 就是这样。点击打印，东西就会包装精美地送到你家门口。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I don't know how that works. Yeah, I don't know how you did that, but it worked. How cool.
turns.zh: 我不知道这怎么运作的。是啊，我不知道你们怎么做到的，但确实成功了。太酷了。

turns.speaker: Melanie Perkins
turns.en: But it's very cool. And so yeah, I guess literally bring these things to life. Oh, we're like launching 3D as well. So all of these things we will be bringing to life literally. And just picking off what is the most strategically important next thing to enable everyone to design anything, to enable everyone to publish anywhere. And we have been doing that for a decade and we'll continue to do that forever more using the latest technology to truly bring people's ideas to life.
turns.zh: 但确实很酷。所以是的，就是要把这些东西真正变现。哦，我们还打算推出3D功能。所以所有这些东西我们都会真正实现。只需挑选出下一个最具战略意义的方向，让每个人都能设计任何东西，都能在任何地方发布内容。我们已经这样做了十年，未来也会一直用最新技术让人们的创意真正落地。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, so this is helpful. So if someone's like, "Oh, will Canva come for my space?" Are people designing thing that was design and also, what was it? Publish?
turns.zh: 好的，这很有帮助。那么如果有人问：“哦，Canva会不会来抢占我们的市场？”人们设计的东西是什么呢？发布吗？

turns.speaker: Melanie Perkins
turns.en: Publishing anywhere.
turns.zh: 在任何地方发布。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. Publishing and designing. Okay. So if you're doing any designing or publishing, watch out.
turns.zh: 好的。设计和发布。好的。所以如果你正在做任何设计或发布工作，得小心点。

turns.speaker: Melanie Perkins
turns.en: From a macro perspective, there was creativity tools and productivity tools. And what Canva really does is we're literally smack bang in the middle of that Venn diagram of creativity and productivity, rather than making our customers have to make a choice between those two suites.
turns.zh: 从宏观角度来看，有创意工具和生产力工具。而Canva真正做的是，我们恰好处于创意和生产力这两个维度的交汇点，而不是让客户在两者之间做选择。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Something I wasn't planning on asking about, but I think it's on everyone's minds. There's always this Figma and Adobe and then there's Canva and there's kind of a bunch of places we could go with this. One is just at the beginning of the journey where a lot of founders try to figure out their wedge and their specific niche. Just how did you think about that? "Here's how we might have a chance to..." I know Figma wasn't even around back then, I don't think. Just how did you approach your early wedge of users?
turns.zh: 我原本没打算问这个问题，但我觉得大家都在思考这个问题。总是有Figma和Adobe，然后还有Canva，关于这方面的讨论有很多。其中一个是创业者在初期试图找到自己的切入点和特定细分市场时会面临的挑战。你当时是如何思考这个问题的？“我们如何才能有机会……” 我知道当时Figma甚至还没出现，对吧？你最初是如何切入用户群体的？

turns.speaker: Melanie Perkins
turns.en: One of the most important things that we did was we didn't really worry about competitors at all. We actually just saw where is there a gap in the market that we can uniquely fill, and what can we solve a problem, a core problem that people currently have today? And so with our first company that was yearbooks in Australia and there wasn't great tools and these yearbook coordinators got thrown in to have to design something and they'd have no design experience. And we spoke to every single customer. We gave them an over the phone tutorial, we understood all of their pain points, we got continuous customer feedback, and then we tried to iterate and improve. (00:51:12): And then when we were thinking about Canva, a few years into that, actually one of the schools said, "I love this product so much. Can I use it to design newsletters?" And they had all sorts of other things that they wanted to use it for, and we kind of looked around and were like, "Oh, there's still nothing on the market." This was a few years into it, that actually does the thing that we're doing, but for all these other things. And so it was much more like where is the gap in the market that people are currently having a pain point? And if you can solve that pain point really well and solve it in such a way that people actually want to pay for it because it is truly solving a real pain point that they have, I think that kind of sets it up for success rather than be a problem or a solution looking for a problem.
turns.zh: 我们做的最重要的一件事就是完全不去担心竞争对手。我们只专注于市场中存在的空白领域，以及如何解决人们当前面临的核心问题。在我们的第一家公司——澳大利亚的年册业务时，当时没有优秀的工具，年册协调员被迫设计年册却毫无设计经验。我们与每位客户进行了深入沟通，提供电话指导，了解他们的痛点，持续收集反馈并不断改进。（00:51:12）几年后，当我们考虑Canva时，实际上有几所学校说：“我太喜欢这个产品了。我能用它设计新闻稿吗？”他们还有各种其他需求。我们环顾四周，发现市场上根本没有满足这些需求的产品。于是我们转向寻找市场空白，解决人们真正痛点的问题。只要能真正解决痛点，让用户愿意为此付费，那么成功就水到渠成，而不是被动地寻找问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So what I'm hearing there is you didn't overthink, "Here's my CP, here's the wedge and the strategy of how we expand into this large thing." It's like, "Here's people with a problem that hasn't been solved in years that we keep seeing. Let's try to solve it."
turns.zh: 所以我听到的是，你们没有过度思考：“这就是我的客户定位，这是我们的切入点和扩展策略。” 而是：“这里有人们多年未解决的痛点，我们不断遇到它。让我们试着解决它。”

turns.speaker: Melanie Perkins
turns.en: Exactly that. And if you take that problem centered approach that helps people to achieve something they actually want to do in the real life, you're probably going to be at a reasonably good spot, especially if it maps to a larger market. That's a particularly great thing. If it only solves one person's problem, that might not be a great company going forward. But if a few people have that same problem... But I think that again, back to that big ladder and that first rung, I think it's better to solve a small number of people's problem really well than trying to solve a large number of people's problem. Not very well at all.
turns.zh: 确实如此。如果你采取以问题为中心的方法，帮助人们在现实生活中实现他们真正想做的事情，你很可能会取得不错的成果，尤其是如果这项技术能对应一个广阔的市场，那就更好了。这真是太棒了。如果它只能解决一个人的问题，那这家公司未来可能不会有太大发展。但如果有几个人面临同样的问题……不过我觉得还是要回归到那个大梯子和第一个台阶的问题。我认为，与其试图解决大量人的问题却做得很差，不如专注于真正为少数人解决问题，并且把这件事做得非常出色。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Something I can't not ask about is just how you think about AI in your product. You mentioned how you integrated or all through the product, just you guys are doing really good stuff with AI. A lot of companies are struggling to find something really that works great. Do you have just a philosophy of, "Here's how we integrate AI into Canva," where it ends up being really helpful and people love it?
turns.zh: 我必须要问的一个问题是，你如何在产品中运用人工智能？你提到你们在整个产品中都进行了整合，人工智能方面做得非常出色。很多公司都在努力寻找真正有效的解决方案。你是否有这样一个理念：“以下是我们将人工智能整合到Canva中的方法”，最终用户对此非常满意？

turns.speaker: Melanie Perkins
turns.en: Your question is actually the answer at the same time. I think being able to integrate it into the product where it actually helps people to get their work done where it genuinely helps them to achieve their goals, and then being really open to listening to your community and hearing what they're loving, what they're struggling with and refining from there I think is really, really important. Just because AI is all the rage and investors really like AI doesn't necessarily mean it should be front and center, but if it can genuinely help your customers to achieve their goals. So the thing that I was mentioning before, enabling people to communicate their ideas and have little friction between those two points, AI is just kind of naturally a very critical part of that equation for us. In fact, it was funny looking back from really old decks. We were trying to do AI before AI was actually a thing because it really was critical to what we were trying to do even in our 2012 deck. You can kind of imagine how AI very much fit into the equation because of exactly what we're trying to do.
turns.zh: 你的问题实际上同时也是答案。我认为，要能将人工智能真正整合到产品中，帮助人们完成工作，真正助力他们实现目标，同时还要真正倾听用户的声音，了解他们的需求和痛点，并据此进行改进，这一点至关重要。仅仅因为人工智能现在很热门，投资者也非常青睐它，并不意味着它就应该成为产品的核心焦点。但如果它能真正帮助客户实现目标，那才是关键所在。所以我之前提到的，让人们能够清晰地传达自己的想法，并且在沟通过程中几乎没有障碍，人工智能自然而然地成为我们解决方案中非常重要的部分。事实上，回顾我们2012年的演示文稿很有趣，当时我们就试图应用人工智能，因为这对我们的目标至关重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm going to keep us on the AI thread and take us to AI Corner, which is a recurring segment on this podcast. So here's the question: what's a way you've found in your personal life and work life to use AI where it ends up being really helpful, something really interesting that people might find useful?
turns.zh: 接下来我们继续讨论人工智能的话题，进入本期播客的固定环节——AI Corner。那么问题来了：在你的个人生活和工作中，有哪些利用人工智能的方法效果显著，特别有趣，值得大家借鉴？

turns.speaker: Melanie Perkins
turns.en: So many things. So AI is often the first. If I'm having an idea, it'll be a first place that I go and explore the idea. And now with Canva, and you can just tag Canva, I can say, "Give me more ideas of this," and it's shockingly great because it has all of the context from the design. It's actually integrated deeply into your workflow. Another really fun thing I do is an AI walk and it's when I just put my ear pods in and then I go for a walk and I just say everything on my mind and I use that to then kind of filter out my thoughts and figure out what are the things I need to action. And it kind of helps again, get out of the weeds and think about things from a more macro perspective rather than from the things that might be in my Slack messages or in my email. It just gives you that sort of helpful vantage point I find. So yeah, so many things.
turns.zh: 太多了。人工智能通常是我的首选。如果我有某个想法，首先会去探索这个想法。现在有了Canva，你只需标记Canva，就能说：“给我更多关于这个的想法”，结果令人惊喜，因为它能整合设计中的所有上下文。它已经深度融入了你的工作流程。另一个很有趣的做法是人工智能漫步，就是戴上耳机出去散步，倾诉脑海中的想法，然后用这些想法来过滤自己的思路，找出需要付诸行动的部分。这又能帮助你跳出繁琐的细节，从更宏观的角度思考问题，而不是被Slack消息或邮件中的琐事所困扰。我发现这真的能提供很有帮助的视角。所以是的，有很多方法。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: For the Voice Note tool, is there a tool that you find useful for that?
turns.zh: 关于语音备忘录工具，有没有你觉得好用的工具呢？

turns.speaker: Melanie Perkins
turns.en: Yeah, I might use Apple Notes or directly into Canva Docs, and then I actually just do the brain dump into Canva Docs and then just summarize them.
turns.zh: 有啊，我可能会用苹果备忘录，或者直接在Canva文档里操作。实际上，我会先在Canva文档里把思路写下来，然后再进行总结。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. And so you just use native microphone-
turns.zh: 明白了。那你用的就是原生的麦克风——

turns.speaker: Melanie Perkins
turns.en: Exactly.
turns.zh: 对啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: ... dictation sort of thing. Nothing fancy?
turns.zh: ……就是那种语音转文字的功能。没有什么特别复杂的功能？

turns.speaker: Melanie Perkins
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay.
turns.zh: 好的。

turns.speaker: Melanie Perkins
turns.en: Yeah, I like it.
turns.zh: 嗯，我挺喜欢的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This reminded me of, you mentioned earlier in our conversation you had this vision board that you said is for 2050. Is that right?
turns.zh: 这让我想起，你之前在我们的对话中提到过你有一个2050年的愿景板。对吗？

turns.speaker: Melanie Perkins
turns.en: Yeah, that's right.
turns.zh: 对啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Can you share something from that vision board?
turns.zh: 能分享一下那个愿景板的内容吗？

turns.speaker: Melanie Perkins
turns.en: I'll tell you why the vision board came about because it's only been in recent months. I did feel like as humanity, we are on a bit of a freight train and that freight training is, I think if we take a lot of visions for a lot of different companies and a lot of things that are happening and you just fast-forward 50 years or you do 2050 and you say, "Are we in a safer world? Is the world the place that we want our kids to grow up in? Is this the humanity that we want?" I didn't feel that the train that we are headed on always feels great. In fact, it scared me quite greatly for a whole host of reasons. And so I sat with that feeling for a little and then I kind of got to work on my 2050 walls and back to the chaos to clarity. (00:56:22): The first thing was riding my 2050 wall and I've really been loving, I've got a whole on the 2050 wall, started with a lot of quotes.
